COMP64702
Revision Lecture
Week 5 – Week 8
Dr. Jingyuan Sun

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
How the exam will test this material
Orientation
Think in terms of skills: recognising, calculating, interpreting, and applying.
Select all that apply
Concept distinctions, true/false traps, 
architecture properties
Numeric calculation
Cosine similarity , TF–IDF , agreement, P /R/F1
Matching / labelling
POS tags, BIO classes, token-level labels
Structure interpretation
Dependency heads, dependents, phrase 
constituents
Fill-in counts

Scenario choice
RAG vs prompting vs fine-tuning; agents and

Reminder: 
 Have a detailed go-through of all previous lecture slides
 Do the practice exam.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
High-yield map
Roadmap
The revision is organised around five examinable clusters.
1. Transformers & representations
RNN comparison, positional encoding, attention, embeddings, TF–IDF
2. LLM training & adaptation
Pretraining, instruction tuning, alignment, MoE, reasoning models
3. Prompting & applications
ICL, CoT, RAG, agents, multimodal systems, safety
4. Sequence labelling
POS tagging, dependency parsing, phrase structure, NER/BIO
5. Evaluation
Gold standards, kappa, precision/recall/F1, averaging, entity-level scoring

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Transformers vs RNN sequence-to-sequence
Transformers
Likely format: select the correct conceptual differences.
Aspect RNN seq2seq Transformer
Processing Sequential over tokens Parallel over input positions
Context Often bottlenecked by hidden 
states; attention can help
Dynamic self-attention over all 
positions
Long-range links Harder due to recurrence Direct pairwise attention paths
Order 
information Implicit in recurrence Needs positional information
What to say in an answer
Transformers do not use recurrence; self-attention lets each 
token build context by attending to other tokens, while 
positional encodings supply order .
Mini practice
Which property makes Transformer encoders easier to 
parallelise than RNN encoders?
A. Causal masking
B. No recurrence over positions
C. Learned output labels
Answer: B
Common trap
Do not claim Transformers have no sequence order; they model order 
after positional information is added.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Positional encoding
Transformers
Self-attention alone treats positions symmetrically; order must be injected.
token embeddings + position vectors order-aware 
representations
Sinusoidal
Fixed function of position
Not learned
Can extrapolate by formula
Classic Transformer design
Learned
Trainable position vectors
Updated with model weights
Common in modern systems
Limited by trained context length
What can be asked?
Identify correct statements about why positional 
encodings are needed and whether they are learned.
Mini practice
Without positional encodings, why are “dogs chase cats” 
and “cats chase dogs” hard for plain self-attention?
Answer: It lacks an explicit signal for token order.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Multi-head attention
Transformers
Likely format: dimensions, projections, and what heads do.
Input
representations
Q/K/V
projections
h attention
heads Concatenate Output
projection
Core idea
Each head attends using its own 
learned projections. Heads can focus 
on different representation 
subspaces or relations.
Dimension rule
A common setup uses d_head = 
d_model / h. The final concatenated 
output returns to d_model before the 
output projection.
Common trap
Heads are not separate slices of the 
input sequence. They process the 
same sequence through different 
projections.
If d_model = 768 and h = 12, what is the typical head dimension?
Answer: 64

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Transformer architecture families
Transformers
Know the attention pattern, use case, and examples.
Encoder-only
Examples: BERT, RoBERTa
Bidirectional self-attention
Best for NLU: classification, tagging, 
extraction
Pretraining often uses MLM-style objectives
Encoder–decoder
Examples: T5, BART
Encoder represents input
Decoder generates output
Decoder uses self-attention + cross-
attention to encoder output
Decoder-only
Examples: GPT-style LLMs
Causal masked self-attention
Prompt understanding and generation occur 
in one left-to-right stream
BERT ≠ autoregressive T5 uses cross-attention GPT uses causal masking

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Word representations & similarity
Representations
Likely format: numeric cosine similarity or conceptual statements about vector methods.
cosine(A, B) = (A · B) / (||A|| ||B||)
Count-based vectors
Term–document or term–term matrices
High-dimensional and sparse
One vector per word type
Can be expensive to store
TF–IDF weighting
Down-weights very common terms
Emphasises informative terms
Does not magically remove sparsity
Contextual meaning
Static vectors struggle with polysemy
Contextual models can represent a word 
differently in different sentences
A=[1,1,0], B=[1,0,0]. Estimate cosine similarity.
Answer: 0.71

LLM Systems
Know the essential components and when RAG is the right choice.
User
query Retriever Knowledge
source
Retrieved
passages

External corpus/vector DB
Retriever

Pretraining from scratch
SFT on a handbook only
A model guessing from parametric

A company Q&A bot must answer from a changing policy manual. Which architecture is usually best?
Answer: Instruction -tuned LLM + RAG.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
LLM pretraining: objective and limitations
LLM Training
Likely format: distinguish training, inference, and what next -token prediction does not guarantee.
Raw text Tokenise Predict next token Cross-entropy loss Update weights
Self-supervised
No manual labels are required. The next 
token in text supplies the training target.
Training vs inference
Training: compare prediction to ground truth 
and update weights.
Inference: choose/sample next token and 
feed it back.
Limitations
Optimises likelihood, not truth. Models may 
hallucinate, repeat biases, or generate unsafe 
content.
Autoregressive factorisation: P(x) = ∏ P(x ₜ | x<ₜ)

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Instruction tuning & alignment
LLM Training
Likely format: identify what each stage changes and what it does not guarantee.
Stage Main purpose
Pretraining General language modelling from raw text
Instruction tuning / SFT Follow natural-language instructions using instruction–
response pairs
RLHF / preference 
optimisation Shift behaviour toward human preferences and safety
DPO / PPO / GRPO Different optimisation routes for preference alignment
HHH target behaviour
Helpful: answer the task
Honest: say what is known/unknown
Harmless: avoid unsafe or abusive outputs
Common trap
Instruction tuning improves following instructions and 
zero/few-shot behaviour , but it does not guarantee factual 
accuracy .
Is instruction tuning inherently the same as RLHF?
Answer: No. It is supervised; RLHF may come afterwards.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
MoE and reasoning models
LLM Training
Likely format: conceptual statements about sparsity, routing, and test-time thinking.
Mixture of Experts (MoE)
Several expert networks share a model. A 
gating/router network selects one or more 
experts for a token.
Pros: sparse activation, faster pretraining, 
scaling.
Cons: more complex, memory heavy , fine-
tuning challenges.
Token
state Router Expert 1 Expert 2 Combine
Reasoning models
They allocate more test -time 
compute by generating 
intermediate reasoning before the 
final response.
Trade-off
Sometimes a smaller model that 
thinks longer can beat a larger 
model that answers immediately, 
but latency/cost increase.
What does “sparse activation” mean in MoE?
Answer: Only a subset of experts runs for each token.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Prompt anatomy and robust prompting
Prompting
Likely format: identify components of a prompt and best practices.
Instruction
What task should the model 
do?
Context
Role, constraints, background
Input data
The text, table, image 
description, or query
Output indicator
Desired format, labels, JSON 
schema, bullets
Best practices
Use clear delimiters around user data
Specify exact output format
Prefer positive instructions
Use examples for custom formats
Check for prompt injection
Mini practice
Improve this prompt:
“Analyse this. ”
Make it exam-ready: add instruction, context, 
input delimiter, output format.
Answer: More specific prompts reduce ambiguity .

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
In-context learning (ICL)
Prompting
Know the difference between examples in the prompt and updating model weights.
Mode What the model receives
Zero-shot Instruction + target input; no examples
One/few-shot Instruction + 1–5 demonstrations + target input
Fine-tuning Training data used to update weights
ICL No gradient descent; temporary working memory only
Memory view
Parametric memory = model weights learned during 
training.
Working memory = current prompt/context window.
Mini practice
Does this use ICL?
Translate to Spanish.
English: good morning → Spanish: buenos días
English: thank you → Spanish:
Answer: Yes — it gives a demonstration in the prompt.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Reasoning prompts and prompt security
Prompting
Likely format: choose the safest or most appropriate prompting strategy.
Chain-of-Thought
Encourages intermediate reasoning before 
the answer . Useful for multi-step math, 
logic, and planning. A short trigger can help, 
but it is not a calculator .
Self-consistency / ToT
Self-consistency samples multiple 
reasoning paths and majority-votes. Tree of 
Thoughts explores branches and 
backtracks.
Prompt injection
Because instructions and data are both text, 
malicious user content can try to override 
the task. Separate instructions from data 
and validate tool use.
For exact arithmetic in an agent, what is safer: pure CoT or a calculator/Python tool?
Answer: Use the external tool and return the observation.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
LLM applications and agents
Applications
Likely format: map an application scenario to the best adaptation strategy.
Core NLP tasks
Summarisation
Structured extraction / NER
Classification and routing
Question answering
Domain applications
Code: unit tests, bug fixing
Legal/finance: RAG for current facts
Healthcare: strict human review
Agents
Brain: LLM
Memory: context/vector store
Tools: APIs, calculator , browser
Loop: plan → act → observe
Deployment bottlenecks
Inference cost, latency , probabilistic reliability, monitoring, safety , prompt 
injection, copyright/IP .
Mini practice
A legal assistant must answer using a changing database of cases. 
Prompting only, RAG, or pretraining from scratch?
Answer: RAG, with careful evaluation and human review.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Multimodal LLMs and evaluation
Applications
Focus on components, evaluation mismatch, and hallucination.
Image / audio Modality
encoder
Connector
projection
LLM
backbone
Text / action
output
Architecture terms
Vision encoder or audio encoder
Projection layer / Q-Former
LLM performs complex reasoning and 
generation
Evaluation issue
Exact string matching can penalise chatty 
correct answers. Modern MLLM evaluation 
often uses rubric-based or LLM-as-judge 
methods.
Hallucination
The model may describe objects or 
relations absent from the image due to 
language priors or compressed visual 
tokens.
Why might a VQA system say “chair” even if no chair is visible near a table?
Answer: Language priors and visual hallucination.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
POS tagging
Sequence 
labelling
Likely format: match Universal POS tags to tokens under a stated interpretation.
What it is
Assign one POS tag to each token after 
tokenisation. The same word can have 
different tags in different contexts.
Tagsets
Penn Treebank: detailed, English-focused.
Universal POS: broader cross-linguistic tags 
such as PRON, AUX, VERB, NOUN, DET , 
PUNCT .
How to decide
Use local context and intended 
meaning. Ask: is the token acting as a 
noun, verb, auxiliary, determiner, etc.?
Tag the ambiguous word only:
“We watched her duck.”
Meaning A: her pet bird. Meaning B: her quickly lower her head.
Answer: A: NOUN; B: VERB

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Dependency parsing
Syntax
Likely format: identify the root, dependents of a head, or the head of a phrase.
head dependent label
(nsubj, obj, mod...)
Reading strategy
1. Find the main predicate/root.
2. Identify direct dependents: subject, object, modifiers.
3. For each modifier, ask which word it describes.
4. Use semantics to resolve attachment ambiguity .
Practice sentence
The analyst emailed the report to Maria.
Root: emailed
Subject dependent: analyst
Object dependent: report
PP target/recipient: Maria
Common trap
Do not confuse the preposition itself with the noun it introduces as the semantic 
head.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Attachment ambiguity
Syntax
The same words can form different structures depending on meaning.
The reviewer read the article with a chart.
Reading A: event modifier
“with a chart” describes how the reviewer read it.
Attach the PP to the verb/read event.
Reading B: noun modifier
“with a chart” describes which article.
Attach the PP to the noun phrase “article” .
Exam-style action: first paraphrase the intended meaning, then draw/read the dependency or phrase structure accordingly.
Answer: Meaning decides attachment.

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Phrase structure parsing
Syntax
Likely format: identify NPs/VPs/PPs from a phrase structure tree.
Constituents
Phrase structure groups words into nested 
constituents rather than head-dependent arcs. 
Typical nodes: S, NP , VP , PP , AdjP , AdvP .
Noun phrases
Centred on a noun or pronoun. May include 
determiners, adjectives, possessives, and 
modifiers.
Not every span
A long sequence is not automatically an 
NP. Check whether it has a 
noun/pronoun head and whether it 
forms a constituent.
Mini practice
In “The student from Leeds solved the puzzle” , name two noun phrases.
Answer: “The student from Leeds”; “Leeds”; “the puzzle”

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Named Entity Recognition (NER) and BIO
Sequence 
labelling
Likely format: count BIO classes or evaluate exact entity spans.
NER task
Identify spans that mention real -world 
entities and assign a type: PER, ORG, 
LOC, DATE, MONEY , etc.
BIO scheme
B-X begins an entity of type X.
I-X continues it.
O means outside any entity.
Class count
For T entity types under BIO:
2T + 1 classes
(B and I for each type, plus O).
If a BIO NER system recognises PER, ORG, LOC, and DATE, how many output classes are needed?
Answer: 2×4 + 1 = 9

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Gold standards, agreement, and Cohen’s Kappa
Evaluation
Likely format: compute observed agreement, expected agreement, then kappa.
Why gold standards?
Benchmarks compare system response 
against reliable reference labels created with 
annotation guidelines.
Observed agreement
Pₐ = proportion of items on which annotators 
agree.
It does not correct for chance agreement.
Expected agreement
Pₑ = chance agreement estimated from 
annotator label distributions.
κ = (Pₐ − Pₑ) / (1 − Pₑ)
If Pₐ = 0.80 and Pₑ = 0.50, compute κ.
Answer: 0.60

COMP64702 Revision Lecture
Precision, recall, F1, and averaging
Evaluation
Likely format: compute scores and explain why accuracy can mislead.
Predicted + Predicted −
Gold + TP FN
Gold − FP TN
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
F1 = 2PR / (P + R)
Averaging
Micro: pool counts
Macro: average class scores 
equally
Weighted: average by class 
support
Entity-level NER
Exact span and type must match. A token -level 
partial overlap is not necessarily a correct entity.
Mini practice
TP=3, FP=1, FN=2. Compute P , R, F1.
Answer: P=.75, R=.60, F1=.667

Wrap-up
Use this as a last-pass plan before the exam.
Memorise formulas
Cosine similarity
TF–IDF ingredients
Cohen’s Kappa
Precision / Recall / F1
Micro vs macro averaging
BIO class count: 2T + 1

Select-all conceptual traps
POS tags under a stated meaning
Dependency heads/dependents
Phrase constituents
NER exact-match counting
Architecture selection scenarios
Avoid common mistakes
Treating ICL as weight updates
Calling instruction tuning “guaranteed 
factuality”
Confusing precision and recall
Counting partial NER spans as correct
Ignoring the stated sentence interpretation
When unsure: define the task, identify the representation, then compute or reason from 
the definition.
